parts.label: b.iii
parts.display_text: A battery has charge capacity 0.55 A h. A circuit draws one pulse of charge 9.4 μC from it each second. Estimate how many years the battery can supply these pulses. Assume its full charge capacity is usable.

answer.text: The available charge is 0.55 × 3600 = 1980 C. Average current = 9.4 × 10⁻⁶ A. Time = 1980/(9.4 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.11 × 10⁸ s, approximately 6.7 years.

parts.given_text: For the same transmitted power, current decreases as transmission voltage increases. Energy lost per second in the cables is I²R.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q15:whole.hint: Connect current to the amount of charge transferred during the relevant time.
notes: Current is I = ΔQ/Δt. For repeated pulses use charge per pulse times pulses per second to obtain average current.
Convert ampere-hours to coulombs using 1 Ah = 3600 C. For microscopic motion use I = nqAv_d, distinguishing number density from total number of carriers.

notes: For a discharging cell, ε = I(R + r) and terminal voltage V = ε − Ir. Internal resistance dissipates some of the source’s power.
A graph of terminal V against I has intercept ε and gradient −r. Check whether the cell is delivering or receiving current before using the voltage sign.

notes: Resistance R = ρL/A. For a circular wire A = πd²/4, so changing diameter affects resistance quadratically.
If volume is conserved during stretching, increasing length also reduces area. Resistivity is a material property at a stated temperature, not the same as resistance.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q7:whole.hint: Find the equivalent resistance of the two parallel lamps, then consider the voltage left across Z.
notes: Two identical lamps of resistance R in parallel have equivalent resistance R/2. Each lamp must have its rated voltage across it.
Z is in series with the parallel pair, so it carries their total current. Use the required voltage division rather than treating all three components as series resistors.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q8:whole.hint: The voltage is unchanged. Choose the power formula with voltage and resistance.
notes: At a fixed voltage, P = V²/R, so power is inversely proportional to resistance.
Do not use the fixed-current conclusion from P = I²R here: the current changes when the resistance changes.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w9:b.hint: Work out what stays fixed when the circuit changes: voltage, current, or neither.
notes: Electrical power is P = VI. For a resistor this can also be I²R or V²/R; choose the form using known quantities.
Energy transferred is Pt for constant power. A filament lamp’s resistance can change with temperature, so do not assume constant resistance unless stated.

notes: For reversible heat transfer at constant temperature, ΔS = Q_rev/T. A warming or cooling reservoir uses the sign of the heat it receives.
